## Wave 49 extended depth layer

This larger tranche adds six extended packets per plan. They deepen the active twenty fields while keeping all mechanics, catalog rows, factions, locations, shelter customs, and late-game institutions provisional and owner-bound.

### Wave 49 extended depth packet 01: willow table compact at Red Willow Sluice

#### Extended field 01 — Premise and canon

The willow table compact begins as a premise audit around Red Willow Sluice. The player is asked to count the lamps before opening the door, but the proposal remains provisional until current source, JSON authority, event producer, host consumer, and ownership ledger are cited. Record the nearest existing seam, the exact absent seam, and the collision to exclude. If the premise is already represented, fold the prose into that owner and retire this packet rather than creating a duplicate.

#### Extended field 02 — Player loop

The loop has six readable beats: arrive at Red Willow Sluice, inspect a practical sign, hear a resident’s account, choose a cost, perform one visible task, and return after the next weather or duty turn. The choice can preserve, delay, redirect, or refuse the request. Show the consequence before explanation. A failure gives information or a bounded recovery task unless the canonical owner defines a terminal result.

#### Extended field 03 — System contract

Route the command through the current owner for Underpass settlements and infrastructure. Define command, event key, inputs, output fact, refusal, fallback, idempotency, and consumer. The packet may touch faction standing, route access, roster duty, shelter archive, relationship, expedition, or ending interpretation only through those authorities. It may not create a private truce score, route graph, calendar, inventory, reputation counter, or parallel legacy record.

#### Extended field 04 — Mechanic

Introduce one mechanic that makes maintenance and trust interact: a concession opens a safer task, a late repair changes a route window, or an honest admission reduces a future surprise. The mechanic should have a threshold, a visible cost, a reversible preparation state, and a deterministic result. The player can test the boundary in a low-risk scene before committing to the late-game version.

#### Extended field 05 — Location lore

At Saltwater Spur, describe who built the room, which flood or fire altered it, who kept the key, and why one wall remains unpainted. Give the player a physical trace, a remembered phrase, a disputed interpretation, and a maintenance action. Returning to the site should show an object moved, repaired, withheld, or shared before any dialogue summarizes the change.

#### Extended field 06 — Shelter lore

The shelter projection keeps a custom tied to the same fact: a cup reserved for a messenger, a bell rung only after consent, a cord tied around a tool, or a bench left open for the missing. The custom has a practical function and a social cost. Its archive text must name the worker who sustains it and the person who objects without reducing either voice to exposition.

#### Extended field 07 — Character voices

Write three distinct voices. A resident of Saltwater Spur notices labor and weather. A representative of Red Willow Works speaks in careful public terms until the cost reaches a family or crew. A witness linked to Saltwater Linekeepers remembers a different sequence. Give each a promise, fear, boundary, apology, refusal, and late callback. Let a minor voice receive a measurable roster, route, archive, or ending consequence.

#### Extended field 08 — Faction politics

The faction layer distinguishes Red Willow Works, Saltwater Linekeepers, Indigo Cinder Tunnelers, and South Kestrel Surveyors by resource, ritual, and risk rather than color. Red Willow Works wants a reliable public record, Saltwater Linekeepers protects a route custom, Indigo Cinder Tunnelers values a scarce repair skill, and South Kestrel Surveyors demands a future witness. None is automatically virtuous. Coalition progress is a projection of existing standing and event facts, with dissent and abstention preserved.

#### Extended field 09 — Story and prose

The side quest opens with an ordinary sentence: someone asks whether the lamp, map, ledger, meal, or signal can wait one more night. The player’s answer changes who performs the task and what is remembered. Use restrained prose, concrete objects, and one silence that another character interprets differently. Add calm, pressure, failure, recovery, refusal, late-arrival, and missing-record variants.

#### Extended field 10 — Late-game system

The late-game form is a major faction or frontier institution that can only appear after several owner-bound facts agree. It may convene a coalition, certify a route, steward a shelter custom, or carry a legacy signal. Its powers are bounded: it can request, witness, schedule, or interpret. It cannot rewrite history, bypass save ownership, or silently convert provisional prose into canon.

#### Extended field 11 — Data and catalog

Candidate content rows for willow table compact carry schema_version, snake_case ID, owner, prerequisites, references, effects, fallback text, localization key, archive policy, retirement note, and missing-data behavior. Link every row to one canonical consumer and one command. Keep Indigo Cinder Pumpway, South Crane Underpass, Indigo Cinder Tunnelers, and South Kestrel Surveyors provisional until catalog aliases and reachability are proven.

#### Extended field 12 — Save and migration

Use the smallest existing save section. Capture the new fact, restore it, migrate older envelopes, tolerate an absent optional row, and make duplicate events idempotent. Define the pre-event, committed, refused, interrupted, and restored states. Do not encode prose branches in a panel cache. A rollback note must identify the event boundary and the owner responsible for undo or compensating projection.

#### Extended field 13 — Deterministic replay

Pin seed, event key, input order, and expected projection. Paired replays must agree on standing, access, route, roster, archive, or ending interpretation. Avoid wall-clock seeds, unordered iteration, hidden random choices, and locale-sensitive sorting. Include a late-arrival replay and a missing-record replay so optional content cannot alter the deterministic core unexpectedly.

#### Extended field 14 — UI and accessibility

The UI exposes a compact action label, expanded explanation, cost, consequence preview, focus order, keyboard and controller back behavior, readable long text, contrast, scaling, non-color cues, and confirmation for irreversible choices. Provide an audio or text alternative. If a record is missing, show a truthful unavailable state and preserve navigation. Archive and map panels consume projections; they do not own decisions.

#### Extended field 15 — Performance and lifecycle

Set budgets for catalog parse, query, event dispatch, archive projection, panel refresh, long text, and return visits. Load high-volume rows lazily, page them without changing order, dispose listeners on close, and avoid repeated full-catalog scans. Add one degradation path for a missing asset or provider. Note the smallest focused host smoke needed if the owner route is eventually implemented.

#### Extended field 16 — Acceptance and handoff

Acceptance requires premise evidence, owner and consumer proof, one reachable player command, save round trip, migration fixture, paired replay, accessibility review, performance notes, and a rollback boundary. The handoff names untouched shared paths and labels this as design scaffolding. The final image is practical: a repaired latch, an amended map, a divided bowl, a chalk mark, a quiet signal, or a door left open by consent.

## Wave 49 capsule layer

These capsules extend the Wave 49 fields with additional playable scaffolds. Each remains provisional, owner-bound, and documentation-only.

### Wave 49 capsule 01: willow-window arbitration at Red Willow Sluice

**Opening and choice.** At **Red Willow Sluice**, the player finds a practical problem that cannot be solved by rhetoric alone: a weather window is closing, a shared tool has two claimants, a missing person may be returning, a night signal is being misread, an apprentice is ready before the shelter is ready, a water ration has been counted twice, a quiet route carries an old debt, or a legacy object must be placed in another person’s hands. The player inspects the evidence, asks for consent, compares accounts, chooses a cost, defers, or leaves. The cost appears before commitment and a refusal keeps a safe return path.

**Authority and mechanic.** Route the action through the current owner for Underpass settlements and infrastructure. Define one command, one event key, one resulting fact, one refusal result, one fallback, and one idempotency rule. A derived readiness view may combine existing standing, relationship, route, roster, shelter, archive, expedition, or ending facts, but it cannot become a second ledger or clock. The mechanic should make an ordinary task consequential: rescheduling a crossing changes who carries a tool, recording a signal changes which watch is asked to stand, or accepting a handover changes who is invited to the next meeting. The player can test the boundary in a low-risk version first.

**Place and shelter lore.** At **Saltwater Spur**, describe the builder, the repair that saved the room, the person who still pays for that repair, and the mark that remains unexplained. At **Indigo Cinder Pumpway**, place a contrasting trace: a patched hinge, a dry shelf, an erased route line, a bell rope, a teaching slate, or a bowl set aside. At **South Crane Underpass**, let a shelter custom make the history useful: a lamp is moved only after consent, a tool is returned sharpened, a guest cup is washed before dawn, or a route name is spoken once and then left unclaimed. Returning to the location shows a changed object before exposition.

**Characters and factions.** A resident speaks in concrete duties and notices who will carry the burden. A representative of **Red Willow Works** uses public language and wants an auditable result. A voice from **Saltwater Linekeepers** protects a custom that looks inefficient until its history is heard. **Indigo Cinder Tunnelers** values a scarce skill, while **South Kestrel Surveyors** asks who will witness the consequence after the player leaves. Give each voice a promise, fear, boundary, apology, refusal, and callback. The late-game factional version may convene a coalition, certify a passage, steward a shelter custom, or preserve a memory, but it may request and witness only through existing authorities.

**Story and prose.** The scene opens with one quiet sentence about work: “The rope is dry enough for one more crossing,” “The cup was left where the missing person could find it,” or “The bell was rung before anyone agreed.” The player’s response changes who performs the task, what the journal remembers, and which later character feels entitled to speak. Add calm, pressure, failure, recovery, refusal, late-arrival, and missing-record variants. Use concrete objects, short silences, and a callback that makes the earlier mechanic visible without turning the packet into a lore lecture.

**Data and content volume.** Candidate rows carry schema_version, snake_case ID, owner, prerequisites, references, effects, fallback text, localization key, archive policy, retirement note, and missing-data behavior. Create arrival, inspection, task, hazard, rest, departure, return, calm, pressure, failure, recovery, refusal, and late-arrival variants. ### Wave 49 capsule 02: shared threshold custody at Red Willow Sluice

**Opening and choice.** At **Red Willow Sluice**, the player finds a practical problem that cannot be solved by rhetoric alone: a weather window is closing, a shared tool has two claimants, a missing person may be returning, a night signal is being misread, an apprentice is ready before the shelter is ready, a water ration has been counted twice, a quiet route carries an old debt, or a legacy object must be placed in another person’s hands. The player inspects the evidence, asks for consent, compares accounts, chooses a cost, defers, or leaves. The cost appears before commitment and a refusal keeps a safe return path.

Define one command, one event key, one resulting fact, one refusal result, one fallback, and one idempotency rule. A derived readiness view may combine existing standing, relationship, route, roster, shelter, archive, expedition, or ending facts, but it cannot become a second ledger or clock. The mechanic should make an ordinary task consequential: rescheduling a crossing changes who carries a tool, recording a signal changes which watch is asked to stand, or accepting a handover changes who is invited to the next meeting. The player can test the boundary in a low-risk version first.

**Place and shelter lore.** At **Saltwater Spur**, describe the builder, the repair that saved the room, the person who still pays for that repair, and the mark that remains unexplained. At **Indigo Cinder Pumpway**, place a contrasting trace: a patched hinge, a dry shelf, an erased route line, a bell rope, a teaching slate, or a bowl set aside. At **South Crane Underpass**, let a shelter custom make the history useful: a lamp is moved only after consent, a tool is returned sharpened, a guest cup is washed before dawn, or a route name is spoken once and then left unclaimed. Returning to the location shows a changed object before exposition.

**Characters and factions.** A resident speaks in concrete duties and notices who will carry the burden. A representative of **Red Willow Works** uses public language and wants an auditable result. A voice from **Saltwater Linekeepers** protects a custom that looks inefficient until its history is heard. **Indigo Cinder Tunnelers** values a scarce skill, while **South Kestrel Surveyors** asks who will witness the consequence after the player leaves. Give each voice a promise, fear, boundary, apology, refusal, and callback. The late-game factional version may convene a coalition, certify a passage, steward a shelter custom, or preserve a memory, but it may request and witness only through existing authorities.

**Story and prose.** The scene opens with one quiet sentence about work: “The rope is dry enough for one more crossing,” “The cup was left where the missing person could find it,” or “The bell was rung before anyone agreed.” The player’s response changes who performs the task, what the journal remembers, and which later character feels entitled to speak. Add calm, pressure, failure, recovery, refusal, late-arrival, and missing-record variants. Use concrete objects, short silences, and a callback that makes the earlier mechanic visible without turning the packet into a lore lecture.

**Data and content volume.** Candidate rows carry schema_version, snake_case ID, owner, prerequisites, references, effects, fallback text, localization key, archive policy, retirement note, and missing-data behavior. Create arrival, inspection, task, hazard, rest, departure, return, calm, pressure, failure, recovery, refusal, and late-arrival variants. Keep the names of **Red Willow Works**, **Saltwater Linekeepers**, **Indigo Cinder Tunnelers**, and **South Kestrel Surveyors** provisional until catalog aliases and reachability are proven. A missing optional row should collapse to a truthful unavailable state rather than alter the deterministic core.

**Persistence and replay.** Capture the smallest new fact through the existing save section. Define pre-action, committed, refused, interrupted, restored, migrated, and duplicate-event states. Pin the campaign seed, event key, input order, and expected projection. Paired replays must agree on standing, access, route, roster, archive, or ending interpretation, including the late-arrival and missing-record cases. Do not use wall-clock seeds, unordered iteration, locale-sensitive sorting, or hidden randomness in prose.

**UI, accessibility, and lifecycle.** Expose a compact action label, expanded explanation, cost, consequence preview, focus order, keyboard/controller close and back, readable long text, contrast, scaling, non-color cues, confirmation for irreversible actions, and text or audio alternatives. Panels consume owner projections and dispose listeners on close. High-volume rows load lazily and page without changing order. Set budgets for parse, query, dispatch, archive projection, refresh, and return visits; document the missing-provider path and the smallest eventual host smoke.

**Acceptance and handoff.** Accept the capsule only with premise evidence, owner and consumer proof, one reachable command, save round trip, migration fixture, paired replay, accessibility review, performance notes, and rollback. The handoff records untouched shared paths and labels the content as design scaffolding. The final image is small and physical: a cord retied, a cup passed over, a map corrected, a signal answered, a tool returned sharper, a meal divided, or a door left open because someone was asked first.

## Wave 50 supplemental receipt

The supplemental packets preserve the active twenty-field structure and broaden the playable content bank. They remain provisional until current catalog, ownership, save, replay, UI, accessibility, performance, and rollback evidence is attached.

## Wave 50 extended depth layer

This larger tranche adds six extended packets per plan. They deepen the active twenty fields while keeping all mechanics, catalog rows, factions, locations, shelter customs, and late-game institutions provisional and owner-bound.

### Wave 50 extended depth packet 01: lantern table compact at Red Lantern Sluice

#### Extended field 01 — Premise and canon

The lantern table compact begins as a premise audit around Red Lantern Sluice. The player is asked to count the lamps before opening the door, but the proposal remains provisional until current source, JSON authority, event producer, host consumer, and ownership ledger are cited. Record the nearest existing seam, the exact absent seam, and the collision to exclude. If the premise is already represented, fold the prose into that owner and retire this packet rather than creating a duplicate.

#### Extended field 02 — Player loop

The loop has six readable beats: arrive at Red Lantern Sluice, inspect a practical sign, hear a resident’s account, choose a cost, perform one visible task, and return after the next weather or duty turn. The choice can preserve, delay, redirect, or refuse the request. Show the consequence before explanation. A failure gives information or a bounded recovery task unless the canonical owner defines a terminal result.

#### Extended field 03 — System contract

Route the command through the current owner for Underpass settlements and infrastructure. Define command, event key, inputs, output fact, refusal, fallback, idempotency, and consumer. The packet may touch faction standing, route access, roster duty, shelter archive, relationship, expedition, or ending interpretation only through those authorities. It may not create a private truce score, route graph, calendar, inventory, reputation counter, or parallel legacy record.

#### Extended field 04 — Mechanic

Introduce one mechanic that makes maintenance and trust interact: a concession opens a safer task, a late repair changes a route window, or an honest admission reduces a future surprise. The mechanic should have a threshold, a visible cost, a reversible preparation state, and a deterministic result. The player can test the boundary in a low-risk scene before committing to the late-game version.

#### Extended field 05 — Location lore

At Slate Orchard Spur, describe who built the room, which flood or fire altered it, who kept the key, and why one wall remains unpainted. Give the player a physical trace, a remembered phrase, a disputed interpretation, and a maintenance action. Returning to the site should show an object moved, repaired, withheld, or shared before any dialogue summarizes the change.

#### Extended field 06 — Shelter lore

The shelter projection keeps a custom tied to the same fact: a cup reserved for a messenger, a bell rung only after consent, a cord tied around a tool, or a bench left open for the missing. The custom has a practical function and a social cost. Its archive text must name the worker who sustains it and the person who objects without reducing either voice to exposition.

#### Extended field 07 — Character voices

Write three distinct voices. A resident of Slate Orchard Spur notices labor and weather. A representative of Red Lantern Works speaks in careful public terms until the cost reaches a family or crew. A witness linked to Slate Orchard Linekeepers remembers a different sequence. Give each a promise, fear, boundary, apology, refusal, and late callback. Let a minor voice receive a measurable roster, route, archive, or ending consequence.

#### Extended field 08 — Faction politics

The faction layer distinguishes Red Lantern Works, Slate Orchard Linekeepers, Cobalt Rain Tunnelers, and South Badger Surveyors by resource, ritual, and risk rather than color. Red Lantern Works wants a reliable public record, Slate Orchard Linekeepers protects a route custom, Cobalt Rain Tunnelers values a scarce repair skill, and South Badger Surveyors demands a future witness. None is automatically virtuous. Coalition progress is a projection of existing standing and event facts, with dissent and abstention preserved.

#### Extended field 09 — Story and prose

The side quest opens with an ordinary sentence: someone asks whether the lamp, map, ledger, meal, or signal can wait one more night. The player’s answer changes who performs the task and what is remembered. Use restrained prose, concrete objects, and one silence that another character interprets differently. Add calm, pressure, failure, recovery, refusal, late-arrival, and missing-record variants.

#### Extended field 10 — Late-game system

The late-game form is a major faction or frontier institution that can only appear after several owner-bound facts agree. It may convene a coalition, certify a route, steward a shelter custom, or carry a legacy signal. Its powers are bounded: it can request, witness, schedule, or interpret. It cannot rewrite history, bypass save ownership, or silently convert provisional prose into canon.

#### Extended field 11 — Data and catalog

Candidate content rows for lantern table compact carry schema_version, snake_case ID, owner, prerequisites, references, effects, fallback text, localization key, archive policy, retirement note, and missing-data behavior. Link every row to one canonical consumer and one command. Keep Cobalt Rain Pumpway, South Badger Underpass, Cobalt Rain Tunnelers, and South Badger Surveyors provisional until catalog aliases and reachability are proven.

#### Extended field 12 — Save and migration

Use the smallest existing save section. Capture the new fact, restore it, migrate older envelopes, tolerate an absent optional row, and make duplicate events idempotent. Define the pre-event, committed, refused, interrupted, and restored states. Do not encode prose branches in a panel cache. A rollback note must identify the event boundary and the owner responsible for undo or compensating projection.

#### Extended field 13 — Deterministic replay

Pin seed, event key, input order, and expected projection. Paired replays must agree on standing, access, route, roster, archive, or ending interpretation. Avoid wall-clock seeds, unordered iteration, hidden random choices, and locale-sensitive sorting. Include a late-arrival replay and a missing-record replay so optional content cannot alter the deterministic core unexpectedly.

#### Extended field 14 — UI and accessibility

The UI exposes a compact action label, expanded explanation, cost, consequence preview, focus order, keyboard and controller back behavior, readable long text, contrast, scaling, non-color cues, and confirmation for irreversible choices. Provide an audio or text alternative. If a record is missing, show a truthful unavailable state and preserve navigation. Archive and map panels consume projections; they do not own decisions.

#### Extended field 15 — Performance and lifecycle

Set budgets for catalog parse, query, event dispatch, archive projection, panel refresh, long text, and return visits. Load high-volume rows lazily, page them without changing order, dispose listeners on close, and avoid repeated full-catalog scans. Add one degradation path for a missing asset or provider. Note the smallest focused host smoke needed if the owner route is eventually implemented.

#### Extended field 16 — Acceptance and handoff

Acceptance requires premise evidence, owner and consumer proof, one reachable player command, save round trip, migration fixture, paired replay, accessibility review, performance notes, and a rollback boundary. The handoff names untouched shared paths and labels this as design scaffolding. The final image is practical: a repaired latch, an amended map, a divided bowl, a chalk mark, a quiet signal, or a door left open by consent.

### Wave 50 capsule 01: frostline arbitration at Red Lantern Sluice

**Opening and choice.** At **Red Lantern Sluice**, the player finds a practical problem that cannot be solved by rhetoric alone: a weather window is closing, a shared tool has two claimants, a missing person may be returning, a night signal is being misread, an apprentice is ready before the shelter is ready, a water ration has been counted twice, a quiet route carries an old debt, or a legacy object must be placed in another person’s hands. The player inspects the evidence, asks for consent, compares accounts, chooses a cost, defers, or leaves. The cost appears before commitment and a refusal keeps a safe return path.

**Authority and mechanic.** Route the action through the current owner for Underpass settlements and infrastructure. Define one command, one event key, one resulting fact, one refusal result, one fallback, and one idempotency rule. A derived readiness view may combine existing standing, relationship, route, roster, shelter, archive, expedition, or ending facts, but it cannot become a second ledger or clock. The mechanic should make an ordinary task consequential: rescheduling a crossing changes who carries a tool, recording a signal changes which watch is asked to stand, or accepting a handover changes who is invited to the next meeting. The player can test the boundary in a low-risk version first.

**Place and shelter lore.** At **Slate Orchard Spur**, describe the builder, the repair that saved the room, the person who still pays for that repair, and the mark that remains unexplained. At **Cobalt Rain Pumpway**, place a contrasting trace: a patched hinge, a dry shelf, an erased route line, a bell rope, a teaching slate, or a bowl set aside. At **South Badger Underpass**, let a shelter custom make the history useful: a lamp is moved only after consent, a tool is returned sharpened, a guest cup is washed before dawn, or a route name is spoken once and then left unclaimed. Returning to the location shows a changed object before exposition.

**Characters and factions.** A resident speaks in concrete duties and notices who will carry the burden. A representative of **Red Lantern Works** uses public language and wants an auditable result. A voice from **Slate Orchard Linekeepers** protects a custom that looks inefficient until its history is heard. **Cobalt Rain Tunnelers** values a scarce skill, while **South Badger Surveyors** asks who will witness the consequence after the player leaves. Give each voice a promise, fear, boundary, apology, refusal, and callback. The late-game factional version may convene a coalition, certify a passage, steward a shelter custom, or preserve a memory, but it may request and witness only through existing authorities.

**Story and prose.** The scene opens with one quiet sentence about work: “The rope is dry enough for one more crossing,” “The cup was left where the missing person could find it,” or “The bell was rung before anyone agreed.” The player’s response changes who performs the task, what the journal remembers, and which later character feels entitled to speak. Add calm, pressure, failure, recovery, refusal, late-arrival, and missing-record variants. Use concrete objects, short silences, and a callback that makes the earlier mechanic visible without turning the packet into a lore lecture.

**Data and content volume.** Candidate rows carry schema_version, snake_case ID, owner, prerequisites, references, effects, fallback text, localization key, archive policy, retirement note, and missing-data behavior. Create arrival, inspection, task, hazard, rest, departure, return, calm, pressure, failure, recovery, refusal, and late-arrival variants. Keep the names of **Red Lantern Works**, **Slate Orchard Linekeepers**, **Cobalt Rain Tunnelers**, and **South Badger Surveyors** provisional until catalog aliases and reachability are proven. A missing optional row should collapse to a truthful unavailable state rather than alter the deterministic core.

**Persistence and replay.** Capture the smallest new fact through the existing save section. Define pre-action, committed, refused, interrupted, restored, migrated, and duplicate-event states. Pin the campaign seed, event key, input order, and expected projection. Paired replays must agree on standing, access, route, roster, archive, or ending interpretation, including the late-arrival and missing-record cases. Do not use wall-clock seeds, unordered iteration, locale-sensitive sorting, or hidden randomness in prose.

**UI, accessibility, and lifecycle.** Expose a compact action label, expanded explanation, cost, consequence preview, focus order, keyboard/controller close and back, readable long text, contrast, scaling, non-color cues, confirmation for irreversible actions, and text or audio alternatives. Panels consume owner projections and dispose listeners on close. High-volume rows load lazily and page without changing order. Set budgets for parse, query, dispatch, archive projection, refresh, and return visits; document the missing-provider path and the smallest eventual host smoke.

**Acceptance and handoff.** Accept the capsule only with premise evidence, owner and consumer proof, one reachable command, save round trip, migration fixture, paired replay, accessibility review, performance notes, and rollback. The handoff records untouched shared paths and labels the content as design scaffolding. The final image is small and physical: a cord retied, a cup passed over, a map corrected, a signal answered, a tool returned sharper, a meal divided, or a door left open because someone was asked first.

The final image is small and physical: a cord retied, a cup passed over, a map corrected, a signal answered, a tool returned sharper, a meal divided, or a door left open because someone was asked first.

The capsule layer remains documentation-only and is ready for premise review, not production promotion.

## Wave 51 supplemental receipt

## Wave 51 extended depth layer

This larger tranche adds six extended packets per plan. They deepen the active twenty fields while keeping all mechanics, catalog rows, factions, locations, shelter customs, and late-game institutions provisional and owner-bound.

### Wave 51 extended depth packet 01: two-seal petition compact at Red Lantern Sluice

#### Extended field 01 — Premise and canon

The two-seal petition compact begins as a premise audit around Red Lantern Sluice. The player is asked to count the lamps before opening the door, but the proposal remains provisional until current source, JSON authority, event producer, host consumer, and ownership ledger are cited. Record the nearest existing seam, the exact absent seam, and the collision to exclude. If the premise is already represented, fold the prose into that owner and retire this packet rather than creating a duplicate.

#### Extended field 02 — Player loop

The loop has six readable beats: arrive at Red Lantern Sluice, inspect a practical sign, hear a resident’s account, choose a cost, perform one visible task, and return after the next weather or duty turn. The choice can preserve, delay, redirect, or refuse the request. Show the consequence before explanation. A failure gives information or a bounded recovery task unless the canonical owner defines a terminal result.

#### Extended field 03 — System contract

Route the command through the current owner for Underpass settlements and infrastructure. Define command, event key, inputs, output fact, refusal, fallback, idempotency, and consumer. The packet may touch faction standing, route access, roster duty, shelter archive, relationship, expedition, or ending interpretation only through those authorities. It may not create a private truce score, route graph, calendar, inventory, reputation counter, or parallel legacy record.

#### Extended field 04 — Mechanic

Introduce one mechanic that makes maintenance and trust interact: a concession opens a safer task, a late repair changes a route window, or an honest admission reduces a future surprise. The mechanic should have a threshold, a visible cost, a reversible preparation state, and a deterministic result. The player can test the boundary in a low-risk scene before committing to the late-game version.

#### Extended field 05 — Location lore

At Slate Orchard Spur, describe who built the room, which flood or fire altered it, who kept the key, and why one wall remains unpainted. Give the player a physical trace, a remembered phrase, a disputed interpretation, and a maintenance action. Returning to the site should show an object moved, repaired, withheld, or shared before any dialogue summarizes the change.

#### Extended field 06 — Shelter lore

The shelter projection keeps a custom tied to the same fact: a cup reserved for a messenger, a bell rung only after consent, a cord tied around a tool, or a bench left open for the missing. The custom has a practical function and a social cost. Its archive text must name the worker who sustains it and the person who objects without reducing either voice to exposition.

#### Extended field 07 — Character voices

Write three distinct voices. A resident of Slate Orchard Spur notices labor and weather. A representative of Red Lantern Works speaks in careful public terms until the cost reaches a family or crew. A witness linked to Slate Orchard Linekeepers remembers a different sequence. Give each a promise, fear, boundary, apology, refusal, and late callback. Let a minor voice receive a measurable roster, route, archive, or ending consequence.

#### Extended field 08 — Faction politics

The faction layer distinguishes Red Lantern Works, Slate Orchard Linekeepers, Cobalt Rain Tunnelers, and Fourth Drain Surveyors by resource, ritual, and risk rather than color. Red Lantern Works wants a reliable public record, Slate Orchard Linekeepers protects a route custom, Cobalt Rain Tunnelers values a scarce repair skill, and Fourth Drain Surveyors demands a future witness. None is automatically virtuous. Coalition progress is a projection of existing standing and event facts, with dissent and abstention preserved.

#### Extended field 09 — Story and prose

The side quest opens with an ordinary sentence: someone asks whether the lamp, map, ledger, meal, or signal can wait one more night. The player’s answer changes who performs the task and what is remembered. Use restrained prose, concrete objects, and one silence that another character interprets differently. Add calm, pressure, failure, recovery, refusal, late-arrival, and missing-record variants.

#### Extended field 10 — Late-game system

The late-game form is a major faction or frontier institution that can only appear after several owner-bound facts agree. It may convene a coalition, certify a route, steward a shelter custom, or carry a legacy signal. Its powers are bounded: it can request, witness, schedule, or interpret. It cannot rewrite history, bypass save ownership, or silently convert provisional prose into canon.

#### Extended field 11 — Data and catalog

Candidate content rows for two-seal petition compact carry schema_version, snake_case ID, owner, prerequisites, references, effects, fallback text, localization key, archive policy, retirement note, and missing-data behavior. Link every row to one canonical consumer and one command. Keep Cobalt Rain Pumpway, South Badger Underpass, Cobalt Rain Tunnelers, and Fourth Drain Surveyors provisional until catalog aliases and reachability are proven.

#### Extended field 12 — Save and migration

Use the smallest existing save section. Capture the new fact, restore it, migrate older envelopes, tolerate an absent optional row, and make duplicate events idempotent. Define the pre-event, committed, refused, interrupted, and restored states. Do not encode prose branches in a panel cache. A rollback note must identify the event boundary and the owner responsible for undo or compensating projection.

#### Extended field 13 — Deterministic replay

Pin seed, event key, input order, and expected projection. Paired replays must agree on standing, access, route, roster, archive, or ending interpretation. Avoid wall-clock seeds, unordered iteration, hidden random choices, and locale-sensitive sorting. Include a late-arrival replay and a missing-record replay so optional content cannot alter the deterministic core unexpectedly.

#### Extended field 14 — UI and accessibility

The UI exposes a compact action label, expanded explanation, cost, consequence preview, focus order, keyboard and controller back behavior, readable long text, contrast, scaling, non-color cues, and confirmation for irreversible choices. Provide an audio or text alternative. If a record is missing, show a truthful unavailable state and preserve navigation. Archive and map panels consume projections; they do not own decisions.

#### Extended field 15 — Performance and lifecycle

Set budgets for catalog parse, query, event dispatch, archive projection, panel refresh, long text, and return visits. Load high-volume rows lazily, page them without changing order, dispose listeners on close, and avoid repeated full-catalog scans. Add one degradation path for a missing asset or provider. Note the smallest focused host smoke needed if the owner route is eventually implemented.

#### Extended field 16 — Acceptance and handoff

Acceptance requires premise evidence, owner and consumer proof, one reachable player command, save round trip, migration fixture, paired replay, accessibility review, performance notes, and a rollback boundary. The handoff names untouched shared paths and labels this as design scaffolding. The final image is practical: a repaired latch, an amended map, a divided bowl, a chalk mark, a quiet signal, or a door left open by consent.

### Wave 51 capsule 01: double-signature arbitration at Red Lantern Sluice

**Opening and choice.** At **Red Lantern Sluice**, the player finds a practical problem that cannot be solved by rhetoric alone: a weather window is closing, a shared tool has two claimants, a missing person may be returning, a night signal is being misread, an apprentice is ready before the shelter is ready, a water ration has been counted twice, a quiet route carries an old debt, or a legacy object must be placed in another person’s hands. The player inspects the evidence, asks for consent, compares accounts, chooses a cost, defers, or leaves. The cost appears before commitment and a refusal keeps a safe return path.

**Authority and mechanic.** Route the action through the current owner for Underpass settlements and infrastructure. Define one command, one event key, one resulting fact, one refusal result, one fallback, and one idempotency rule. A derived readiness view may combine existing standing, relationship, route, roster, shelter, archive, expedition, or ending facts, but it cannot become a second ledger or clock. The mechanic should make an ordinary task consequential: rescheduling a crossing changes who carries a tool, recording a signal changes which watch is asked to stand, or accepting a handover changes who is invited to the next meeting. The player can test the boundary in a low-risk version first.

**Place and shelter lore.** At **Slate Orchard Spur**, describe the builder, the repair that saved the room, the person who still pays for that repair, and the mark that remains unexplained. At **Cobalt Rain Pumpway**, place a contrasting trace: a patched hinge, a dry shelf, an erased route line, a bell rope, a teaching slate, or a bowl set aside. At **South Badger Underpass**, let a shelter custom make the history useful: a lamp is moved only after consent, a tool is returned sharpened, a guest cup is washed before dawn, or a route name is spoken once and then left unclaimed. Returning to the location shows a changed object before exposition.

**Characters and factions.** A resident speaks in concrete duties and notices who will carry the burden. A representative of **Red Lantern Works** uses public language and wants an auditable result. A voice from **Slate Orchard Linekeepers** protects a custom that looks inefficient until its history is heard. **Cobalt Rain Tunnelers** values a scarce skill, while **Fourth Drain Surveyors** asks who will witness the consequence after the player leaves. Give each voice a promise, fear, boundary, apology, refusal, and callback. The late-game factional version may convene a coalition, certify a passage, steward a shelter custom, or preserve a memory, but it may request and witness only through existing authorities.

**Story and prose.** The scene opens with one quiet sentence about work: “The rope is dry enough for one more crossing,” “The cup was left where the missing person could find it,” or “The bell was rung before anyone agreed.” The player’s response changes who performs the task, what the journal remembers, and which later character feels entitled to speak. Add calm, pressure, failure, recovery, refusal, late-arrival, and missing-record variants. Use concrete objects, short silences, and a callback that makes the earlier mechanic visible without turning the packet into a lore lecture.

**Data and content volume.** Candidate rows carry schema_version, snake_case ID, owner, prerequisites, references, effects, fallback text, localization key, archive policy, retirement note, and missing-data behavior. Create arrival, inspection, task, hazard, rest, departure, return, calm, pressure, failure, recovery, refusal, and late-arrival variants. Keep the names of **Red Lantern Works**, **Slate Orchard Linekeepers**, **Cobalt Rain Tunnelers**, and **Fourth Drain Surveyors** provisional until catalog aliases and reachability are proven. A missing optional row should collapse to a truthful unavailable state rather than alter the deterministic core.

**Persistence and replay.** Capture the smallest new fact through the existing save section. Define pre-action, committed, refused, interrupted, restored, migrated, and duplicate-event states. Pin the campaign seed, event key, input order, and expected projection. Paired replays must agree on standing, access, route, roster, archive, or ending interpretation, including the late-arrival and missing-record cases. Do not use wall-clock seeds, unordered iteration, locale-sensitive sorting, or hidden randomness in prose.

**UI, accessibility, and lifecycle.** Expose a compact action label, expanded explanation, cost, consequence preview, focus order, keyboard/controller close and back, readable long text, contrast, scaling, non-color cues, confirmation for irreversible actions, and text or audio alternatives. Panels consume owner projections and dispose listeners on close. High-volume rows load lazily and page without changing order. Set budgets for parse, query, dispatch, archive projection, refresh, and return visits; document the missing-provider path and the smallest eventual host smoke.

**Acceptance and handoff.** Accept the capsule only with premise evidence, owner and consumer proof, one reachable command, save round trip, migration fixture, paired replay, accessibility review, performance notes, and rollback. The handoff records untouched shared paths and labels the content as design scaffolding. The final image is small and physical: a cord retied, a cup passed over, a map corrected, a signal answered, a tool returned sharper, a meal divided, or a door left open because someone was asked first.

## Wave 51 late-game faction and playable arc dossier — The Underway Custodians

**Canon status.** The Underway Custodians is a proposed major late-game faction, not an established catalog entity. Search the current narrative catalog, previous plan index, ownership ledger, and integration queue before implementation. If its role duplicates an existing organization, merge the useful quest material into that owner or retire this faction. The locations, leaders, mechanics, and story outcomes in this dossier remain provisional.

### Mandate and opening incident

A late-game maintenance compact that may request inspections, publish a hazard projection, coordinate a repair crew, and schedule a safe passage through existing expedition, map, weather, vehicle, and shelter owners. It cannot add a private route graph, a hidden travel clock, or direct vehicle orders. At Low Bell Sluice a handwheel returns smoothly but the downstream chalk mark has moved. Sella says the pressure report is stale; Pavo says the handle is warning them. The player must compare sound, water stain, map annotation, and the last repair record. The route is not opened by finding a secret switch; it is made safer by agreeing what is known and what remains uncertain.

### Five-quest playable spine

Quest 1 — The Wheel That Turned Too Easily: inspect the sluice, record a controlled test, or decline a risky test and ask for a second gauge. Quest 2 — Three Marks in the Culvert: follow Painted Culvert Spur and reconcile a wayfinding mark, a shelter chalk line, and a survey note without creating a duplicate node. Quest 3 — The Dry Room Below: discover that a rest chamber is being used as a tool store; let its occupants choose what can be moved before the repair crew arrives. Quest 4 — The Apprentice’s Sound: Pavo demonstrates a safe listening check, and the player decides whether the technique becomes public instruction or stays attached to his name. Quest 5 — The Underway Compact: convene route custodians to assign an inspection, publish uncertainty, delay traffic, or leave the corridor closed. Later return shows a repaired latch, a new warning phrase, or a route still marked unknown.

### Faction structure and late-game function

The Custodians divide into the Open Map crew, which believes uncertainty should be visible; the Quiet Repair crew, which fears warnings will strand families; and the Load-Bearers, who insist that any passage plan name the people performing inspection and carrying material. Their conflict is about acceptable evidence and duty, not competing cartography authorities. Every route display remains a projection of current map and expedition facts. The late-game compact works through a periodic inspection scene, not a new simulation subsystem. It can ask the player to allocate a skilled survivor through current roster and duty commands, inspect existing weather and hazard projections, and accept a route state from its owner. It produces no new travel edges. A single repair can change the usability or hazard context of an existing location only if the current map/expedition contract supports that result. Missing support leaves the planned route unavailable with an actionable explanation.

### Named character personalities

Sella speaks in measurements and deliberately leaves one notch uncut when confidence is low. Pavo notices vibrations other people dismiss and is embarrassed when asked to explain them in front of senior workers. A third recurring character, Dena Sol, maintains a rest chamber and objects when map makers name rooms after the people who discovered them. Sella’s arc shifts from precise marks to explicit uncertainty; Pavo’s shifts from private skill to consent-based teaching. Dena’s shelter work changes who is offered rest first after a long crossing.

### Diegetic prose and scene variants

Quest prose: “The wheel turned without complaint. That was what made Sella step back.” “Pavo held the handle and asked everyone else to stop talking.” “On the new map, the room had no name. Dena said that was accurate for now.” Include silent visual traces for noise-sensitive play, text description for directional audio, non-color hazard symbols, and a safe exit from every inspection choice. A failed test informs rather than kills the player unless current survival rules already determine risk.

### Existing-system contract, save, and replay

Use current map nodes and references as identifiers; never let the Custodians author mutable parallel edges. Any inspection result is a fact routed through the existing expedition/weather/communications contract. A candidate row records location reference, inspection type, evidence source, outcome, owner event, and fallback. Stateful results use current save owners, stable seeded ordering, and a migration default of unknown. The data validator must reject dangling location IDs and impossible severity ranges.

### UI, accessibility, performance, and acceptance

The map UI displays condition, confidence, source, age, route owner, and a one-line action. It differentiates “not surveyed” from “unsafe” and “temporarily closed.” Controller focus moves from route title to source evidence, inspection action, recovery alternative, and back. Use visible text and icon shape as redundant cues. Performance needs cached projection invalidation by relevant events rather than repeated all-node scans; the Custodians do not keep their own map cache. All places and mechanics remain candidates pending premise, catalog, claim, save, and runtime review.

**Promotion boundary.** The faction becomes implementation-ready only after a current-source premise check names its owner, consumer, event producer, data schema, save path if stateful, host route, and rollback seam. No faction name or narrative outcome here is canon until that review is complete.

## Wave 52 supplemental receipt

## Wave 52 extended depth layer

This larger tranche adds six extended packets per plan. They deepen the active twenty fields while keeping all mechanics, catalog rows, factions, locations, shelter customs, and late-game institutions provisional and owner-bound.

### Wave 52 extended depth packet 01: two-seal petition compact at Red Lantern Sluice

#### Extended field 01 — Premise and canon

The two-seal petition compact begins as a premise audit around Red Lantern Sluice. The player is asked to count the lamps before opening the door, but the proposal remains provisional until current source, JSON authority, event producer, host consumer, and ownership ledger are cited. Record the nearest existing seam, the exact absent seam, and the collision to exclude. If the premise is already represented, fold the prose into that owner and retire this packet rather than creating a duplicate.

#### Extended field 02 — Player loop

The loop has six readable beats: arrive at Red Lantern Sluice, inspect a practical sign, hear a resident’s account, choose a cost, perform one visible task, and return after the next weather or duty turn. The choice can preserve, delay, redirect, or refuse the request. Show the consequence before explanation. A failure gives information or a bounded recovery task unless the canonical owner defines a terminal result.

#### Extended field 03 — System contract

Route the command through the current owner for Underpass settlements and infrastructure. Define command, event key, inputs, output fact, refusal, fallback, idempotency, and consumer. The packet may touch faction standing, route access, roster duty, shelter archive, relationship, expedition, or ending interpretation only through those authorities. It may not create a private truce score, route graph, calendar, inventory, reputation counter, or parallel legacy record.

#### Extended field 04 — Mechanic

Introduce one mechanic that makes maintenance and trust interact: a concession opens a safer task, a late repair changes a route window, or an honest admission reduces a future surprise. The mechanic should have a threshold, a visible cost, a reversible preparation state, and a deterministic result. The player can test the boundary in a low-risk scene before committing to the late-game version.

#### Extended field 05 — Location lore

At Slate Orchard Spur, describe who built the room, which flood or fire altered it, who kept the key, and why one wall remains unpainted. Give the player a physical trace, a remembered phrase, a disputed interpretation, and a maintenance action. Returning to the site should show an object moved, repaired, withheld, or shared before any dialogue summarizes the change.

#### Extended field 06 — Shelter lore

The shelter projection keeps a custom tied to the same fact: a cup reserved for a messenger, a bell rung only after consent, a cord tied around a tool, or a bench left open for the missing. The custom has a practical function and a social cost. Its archive text must name the worker who sustains it and the person who objects without reducing either voice to exposition.

#### Extended field 07 — Character voices

Write three distinct voices. A resident of Slate Orchard Spur notices labor and weather. A representative of Red Lantern Works speaks in careful public terms until the cost reaches a family or crew. A witness linked to Slate Orchard Linekeepers remembers a different sequence. Give each a promise, fear, boundary, apology, refusal, and late callback. Let a minor voice receive a measurable roster, route, archive, or ending consequence.

#### Extended field 08 — Faction politics

The faction layer distinguishes Red Lantern Works, Slate Orchard Linekeepers, Cobalt Rain Tunnelers, and Kiln Surveyors by resource, ritual, and risk rather than color. Red Lantern Works wants a reliable public record, Slate Orchard Linekeepers protects a route custom, Cobalt Rain Tunnelers values a scarce repair skill, and Kiln Surveyors demands a future witness. None is automatically virtuous. Coalition progress is a projection of existing standing and event facts, with dissent and abstention preserved.

#### Extended field 09 — Story and prose

The side quest opens with an ordinary sentence: someone asks whether the lamp, map, ledger, meal, or signal can wait one more night. The player’s answer changes who performs the task and what is remembered. Use restrained prose, concrete objects, and one silence that another character interprets differently. Add calm, pressure, failure, recovery, refusal, late-arrival, and missing-record variants.

#### Extended field 10 — Late-game system

The late-game form is a major faction or frontier institution that can only appear after several owner-bound facts agree. It may convene a coalition, certify a route, steward a shelter custom, or carry a legacy signal. Its powers are bounded: it can request, witness, schedule, or interpret. It cannot rewrite history, bypass save ownership, or silently convert provisional prose into canon.

#### Extended field 11 — Data and catalog

Candidate content rows for two-seal petition compact carry schema_version, snake_case ID, owner, prerequisites, references, effects, fallback text, localization key, archive policy, retirement note, and missing-data behavior. Link every row to one canonical consumer and one command. Keep Cobalt Rain Pumpway, South Badger Underpass, Cobalt Rain Tunnelers, and Kiln Surveyors provisional until catalog aliases and reachability are proven.

#### Extended field 12 — Save and migration

Use the smallest existing save section. Capture the new fact, restore it, migrate older envelopes, tolerate an absent optional row, and make duplicate events idempotent. Define the pre-event, committed, refused, interrupted, and restored states. Do not encode prose branches in a panel cache. A rollback note must identify the event boundary and the owner responsible for undo or compensating projection.

#### Extended field 13 — Deterministic replay

Pin seed, event key, input order, and expected projection. Paired replays must agree on standing, access, route, roster, archive, or ending interpretation. Avoid wall-clock seeds, unordered iteration, hidden random choices, and locale-sensitive sorting. Include a late-arrival replay and a missing-record replay so optional content cannot alter the deterministic core unexpectedly.

#### Extended field 14 — UI and accessibility

The UI exposes a compact action label, expanded explanation, cost, consequence preview, focus order, keyboard and controller back behavior, readable long text, contrast, scaling, non-color cues, and confirmation for irreversible choices. Provide an audio or text alternative. If a record is missing, show a truthful unavailable state and preserve navigation. Archive and map panels consume projections; they do not own decisions.

#### Extended field 15 — Performance and lifecycle

Set budgets for catalog parse, query, event dispatch, archive projection, panel refresh, long text, and return visits. Load high-volume rows lazily, page them without changing order, dispose listeners on close, and avoid repeated full-catalog scans. Add one degradation path for a missing asset or provider. Note the smallest focused host smoke needed if the owner route is eventually implemented.

#### Extended field 16 — Acceptance and handoff

Acceptance requires premise evidence, owner and consumer proof, one reachable player command, save round trip, migration fixture, paired replay, accessibility review, performance notes, and a rollback boundary. The handoff names untouched shared paths and labels this as design scaffolding. The final image is practical: a repaired latch, an amended map, a divided bowl, a chalk mark, a quiet signal, or a door left open by consent.

### Wave 52 capsule 01: double-signature arbitration at Red Lantern Sluice

**Opening and choice.** At **Red Lantern Sluice**, the player finds a practical problem that cannot be solved by rhetoric alone: a weather window is closing, a shared tool has two claimants, a missing person may be returning, a night signal is being misread, an apprentice is ready before the shelter is ready, a water ration has been counted twice, a quiet route carries an old debt, or a legacy object must be placed in another person’s hands. The player inspects the evidence, asks for consent, compares accounts, chooses a cost, defers, or leaves. The cost appears before commitment and a refusal keeps a safe return path.

**Authority and mechanic.** Route the action through the current owner for Underpass settlements and infrastructure. Define one command, one event key, one resulting fact, one refusal result, one fallback, and one idempotency rule. A derived readiness view may combine existing standing, relationship, route, roster, shelter, archive, expedition, or ending facts, but it cannot become a second ledger or clock. The mechanic should make an ordinary task consequential: rescheduling a crossing changes who carries a tool, recording a signal changes which watch is asked to stand, or accepting a handover changes who is invited to the next meeting. The player can test the boundary in a low-risk version first.

**Place and shelter lore.** At **Slate Orchard Spur**, describe the builder, the repair that saved the room, the person who still pays for that repair, and the mark that remains unexplained. At **Cobalt Rain Pumpway**, place a contrasting trace: a patched hinge, a dry shelf, an erased route line, a bell rope, a teaching slate, or a bowl set aside. At **South Badger Underpass**, let a shelter custom make the history useful: a lamp is moved only after consent, a tool is returned sharpened, a guest cup is washed before dawn, or a route name is spoken once and then left unclaimed. Returning to the location shows a changed object before exposition.

**Characters and factions.** A resident speaks in concrete duties and notices who will carry the burden. A representative of **Red Lantern Works** uses public language and wants an auditable result. A voice from **Slate Orchard Linekeepers** protects a custom that looks inefficient until its history is heard. **Cobalt Rain Tunnelers** values a scarce skill, while **Kiln Surveyors** asks who will witness the consequence after the player leaves. Give each voice a promise, fear, boundary, apology, refusal, and callback. The late-game factional version may convene a coalition, certify a passage, steward a shelter custom, or preserve a memory, but it may request and witness only through existing authorities.

**Story and prose.** The scene opens with one quiet sentence about work: “The rope is dry enough for one more crossing,” “The cup was left where the missing person could find it,” or “The bell was rung before anyone agreed.” The player’s response changes who performs the task, what the journal remembers, and which later character feels entitled to speak. Add calm, pressure, failure, recovery, refusal, late-arrival, and missing-record variants. Use concrete objects, short silences, and a callback that makes the earlier mechanic visible without turning the packet into a lore lecture.

**Data and content volume.** Candidate rows carry schema_version, snake_case ID, owner, prerequisites, references, effects, fallback text, localization key, archive policy, retirement note, and missing-data behavior. Create arrival, inspection, task, hazard, rest, departure, return, calm, pressure, failure, recovery, refusal, and late-arrival variants. Keep the names of **Red Lantern Works**, **Slate Orchard Linekeepers**, **Cobalt Rain Tunnelers**, and **Kiln Surveyors** provisional until catalog aliases and reachability are proven. A missing optional row should collapse to a truthful unavailable state rather than alter the deterministic core.

**Persistence and replay.** Capture the smallest new fact through the existing save section. Define pre-action, committed, refused, interrupted, restored, migrated, and duplicate-event states. Pin the campaign seed, event key, input order, and expected projection. Paired replays must agree on standing, access, route, roster, archive, or ending interpretation, including the late-arrival and missing-record cases. Do not use wall-clock seeds, unordered iteration, locale-sensitive sorting, or hidden randomness in prose.

**UI, accessibility, and lifecycle.** Expose a compact action label, expanded explanation, cost, consequence preview, focus order, keyboard/controller close and back, readable long text, contrast, scaling, non-color cues, confirmation for irreversible actions, and text or audio alternatives. Panels consume owner projections and dispose listeners on close. High-volume rows load lazily and page without changing order. Set budgets for parse, query, dispatch, archive projection, refresh, and return visits; document the missing-provider path and the smallest eventual host smoke.

**Acceptance and handoff.** Accept the capsule only with premise evidence, owner and consumer proof, one reachable command, save round trip, migration fixture, paired replay, accessibility review, performance notes, and rollback. The handoff records untouched shared paths and labels the content as design scaffolding. The final image is small and physical: a cord retied, a cup passed over, a map corrected, a signal answered, a tool returned sharper, a meal divided, or a door left open because someone was asked first.

## Wave 52 late-game faction and playable arc dossier — The Floodline Mutual

**Canon and collision status.** The Floodline Mutual is proposed major late-game content, not an established faction. Its role must be compared with current catalog records, source owners, live plan index, integration queue, and path claims. If it duplicates a current faction, archive, route, education, or ending contract, merge its usable quests into that authority or retire the proposal. Locations, characters, and outcomes remain provisional.

### Mandate and opening incident at Ashline Siphon

The Floodline Mutual is a proposed late-game water-and-evacuation faction formed by families who live near seasonal underpass surges. It focuses on deciding when a shelter moves people, supplies, or working shifts above the water mark. It has no independent route graph or stores ledger. It requests a hazard projection from current weather and water owners, then asks settlements to opt into a prepared transfer using existing inventory, roster, expedition, and shelter commands. At Ashline Siphon, an old red cord hangs above a door frame. The cord marked the height at which one family moved its sleeping mats, but a newer resident says the mark is lower than last year’s water. The player can compare visible stains, a pump log, and the survey note; no one may trigger a dangerous test just to make the map certain. The decision is whether to prepare, move now, or accept a bounded wait with a named check-in.

### Five-quest story spine

Quest 1 — The Cord above the Door: measure the mark and record uncertainty; use two non-destructive sources before suggesting action. Quest 2 — A Room for the Dry Tools: travel to Brickroot Cut and ask which equipment may move first without emptying an occupied sleeping room. Quest 3 — The Night Shift List: at West Coil Passage, negotiate who can cover the pump while families relocate; check fatigue and duty owners rather than assigning a hidden crew. Quest 4 — One Cart, Two Shelters: compare a child’s medical supplies and a repair kit, then find a second trip or ask which need can wait. Quest 5 — The Floodline Pact: the Mutual convenes at Lower Kiln Walk to choose a preparation threshold, a public warning, and a review time. Outcomes include prepared, moved, deferred, or declined; the player later sees whether a room was dried, a shift relieved, or a marker revised.

### Faction tensions and late-game leverage

The Low-Mark households want early warnings because they remember being trapped; the Dry-Store workers fear that repeated false alarms will ruin equipment and trust; the Upper-Room residents object to becoming the default refuge for every flood season. The faction’s major late-game role is to negotiate mutual aid across these interests. It can request a move or publish a hazard note, but it cannot compel evacuation or calculate an unseen global flood calendar. The faction’s practical strength comes from convening people who already have authority over the relevant task. Its leverage is a credible witness, a better-timed request, or an option to defer; it gains no hidden territory, reputation track, clock, inventory pool, or ending state. A player can refuse membership and still complete the surrounding story.

### Character voices and relationships

Nima Vos ties the red cord and carries a small notebook of heights, but she refuses to be introduced as “the flood survivor.” Teren Ash maintains the siphon and insists that a pump sound is evidence only when paired with inspection. Vika Ren lives in an upper room and keeps a list of who has been asked to host twice. Each voice distinguishes duty from consent; they disagree about when preparation becomes pressure. Recurring dialogue should show this through changed duties and everyday habits: who gets asked first, who moves a cup, who checks a latch, who gets an uninterrupted turn to speak. Relationship consequences are routed through the existing relationship owner; avoid numerical affinity gates invented for this faction.

### Prose and playable variation

Prose lines: “The cord stopped short of the newer stain.” “Nima lifted the notebook but did not open it.” “Vika asked who had slept upstairs last time and who had thanked them.” Side quests show practical consequences before summaries: dry blankets are hung, a shift changes hands, a tool cart leaves a room, or a family returns to a threshold they chose. Failure branches reveal uncertainty and offer a safe return visit. Author scene variants for ordinary conditions, pressure, failure, recovery, refusal, late arrival, missing evidence, and changed relationships. Keep each variant tied to one observable event or prop. Side quests should expose costs and agency before interpreting the choice. Do not make lore access depend on accepting the faction’s interpretation.

### New feature and system proposal

The new system proposal is a flood-preparation review built on current hazard projections and existing commands. It produces a staged checklist (inspect, prepare, move, review) but stores no duplicate level or flood clock. A candidate event references a known location and current weather/water fact, then leaves inventory, needs, roster, and route changes to their own owners. If the water/hazard owner has no supported API, retain the quest as narrative scaffolding and do not invent a local forecast. The proposal should be implemented as content and projection over existing owners unless a future architecture decision explicitly authorizes a new owner. Describe command, event, consumer, save contract if stateful, migration, deterministic replay, and rollback before data is added. If the necessary premise is absent, retain the design note and omit mutable state.

### UI, accessibility, performance, and verification

The map and shelter interface use “observed mark,” “reported mark,” and “unverified” rather than a single unexplained danger color. Every action states who will carry material and what room will be affected. Support text and icon shapes, keyboard/controller order, zoom, reduced-motion presentation, and a close/back path that preserves an unsubmitted preparation choice. Load only visible shelter and location rows; cache invalidation follows relevant owner events. Validate with save round-trip and replay only if stateful implementation is approved. The dossier is ready for implementation review only after evidence identifies exact source paths, API or data families, event producers, host routes, save owners, and unclaimed implementation paths. Test only the focused owner contract, data validator, save round-trip, and deterministic replay that the approved seam requires. No full suite is implied by this plan.


## Continuation Wave 53 — Passes 571–581

This synchronized continuation keeps Fields 11–20 active. It adds new provisional factions, late-game organizations, locations, shelter customs, survivor voices, mechanics, side quests, UI/UX scaffolds, and performance or replay gates without claiming production implementation or creating parallel mutable state.

## Wave 53 supplemental receipt

The supplemental packets preserve the active twenty-field structure and broaden the playable content bank. They remain provisional until current catalog, ownership, save, replay, UI, accessibility, performance, and rollback evidence is attached.


## Wave 53 extended depth layer

This larger tranche adds six extended packets per plan. They deepen the active twenty fields while keeping all mechanics, catalog rows, factions, locations, shelter customs, and late-game institutions provisional and owner-bound.

### Wave 53 extended depth packet 01: copperline witness table at Red Lantern Sluice

#### Extended field 01 — Premise and canon

The copperline witness table begins as a premise audit around Red Lantern Sluice. The player is asked to count the lamps before opening the door, but the proposal remains provisional until current source, JSON authority, event producer, host consumer, and ownership ledger are cited. Record the nearest existing seam, the exact absent seam, and the collision to exclude. If the premise is already represented, fold the prose into that owner and retire this packet rather than creating a duplicate.

#### Extended field 02 — Player loop

The loop has six readable beats: arrive at Red Lantern Sluice, inspect a practical sign, hear a resident’s account, choose a cost, perform one visible task, and return after the next weather or duty turn. The choice can preserve, delay, redirect, or refuse the request. Show the consequence before explanation. A failure gives information or a bounded recovery task unless the canonical owner defines a terminal result.

#### Extended field 03 — System contract

Route the command through the current owner for Underpass settlements and infrastructure. Define command, event key, inputs, output fact, refusal, fallback, idempotency, and consumer. The packet may touch faction standing, route access, roster duty, shelter archive, relationship, expedition, or ending interpretation only through those authorities. It may not create a private truce score, route graph, calendar, inventory, reputation counter, or parallel legacy record.

#### Extended field 04 — Mechanic

Introduce one mechanic that makes maintenance and trust interact: a concession opens a safer task, a late repair changes a route window, or an honest admission reduces a future surprise. The mechanic should have a threshold, a visible cost, a reversible preparation state, and a deterministic result. The player can test the boundary in a low-risk scene before committing to the late-game version.

#### Extended field 05 — Location lore

At Slate Orchard Spur, describe who built the room, which flood or fire altered it, who kept the key, and why one wall remains unpainted. Give the player a physical trace, a remembered phrase, a disputed interpretation, and a maintenance action. Returning to the site should show an object moved, repaired, withheld, or shared before any dialogue summarizes the change.

#### Extended field 06 — Shelter lore

The shelter projection keeps a custom tied to the same fact: a cup reserved for a messenger, a bell rung only after consent, a cord tied around a tool, or a bench left open for the missing. The custom has a practical function and a social cost. Its archive text must name the worker who sustains it and the person who objects without reducing either voice to exposition.

#### Extended field 07 — Character voices

Write three distinct voices. A resident of Slate Orchard Spur notices labor and weather. A representative of Red Lantern Works speaks in careful public terms until the cost reaches a family or crew. A witness linked to Slate Orchard Linekeepers remembers a different sequence. Give each a promise, fear, boundary, apology, refusal, and late callback. Let a minor voice receive a measurable roster, route, archive, or ending consequence.

#### Extended field 08 — Faction politics

The faction layer distinguishes Red Lantern Works, Slate Orchard Linekeepers, Cobalt Rain Tunnelers, and Furnace Walk Surveyors by resource, ritual, and risk rather than color. Red Lantern Works wants a reliable public record, Slate Orchard Linekeepers protects a route custom, Cobalt Rain Tunnelers values a scarce repair skill, and Furnace Walk Surveyors demands a future witness. None is automatically virtuous. Coalition progress is a projection of existing standing and event facts, with dissent and abstention preserved.

#### Extended field 09 — Story and prose

The side quest opens with an ordinary sentence: someone asks whether the lamp, map, ledger, meal, or signal can wait one more night. The player’s answer changes who performs the task and what is remembered. Use restrained prose, concrete objects, and one silence that another character interprets differently. Add calm, pressure, failure, recovery, refusal, late-arrival, and missing-record variants.

#### Extended field 10 — Late-game system

The late-game form is a major faction or frontier institution that can only appear after several owner-bound facts agree. It may convene a coalition, certify a route, steward a shelter custom, or carry a legacy signal. Its powers are bounded: it can request, witness, schedule, or interpret. It cannot rewrite history, bypass save ownership, or silently convert provisional prose into canon.

#### Extended field 11 — Data and catalog

Candidate content rows for copperline witness table carry schema_version, snake_case ID, owner, prerequisites, references, effects, fallback text, localization key, archive policy, retirement note, and missing-data behavior. Link every row to one canonical consumer and one command. Keep Cobalt Rain Pumpway, South Badger Underpass, Cobalt Rain Tunnelers, and Furnace Walk Surveyors provisional until catalog aliases and reachability are proven.

#### Extended field 12 — Save and migration

Use the smallest existing save section. Capture the new fact, restore it, migrate older envelopes, tolerate an absent optional row, and make duplicate events idempotent. Define the pre-event, committed, refused, interrupted, and restored states. Do not encode prose branches in a panel cache. A rollback note must identify the event boundary and the owner responsible for undo or compensating projection.

#### Extended field 13 — Deterministic replay

Pin seed, event key, input order, and expected projection. Paired replays must agree on standing, access, route, roster, archive, or ending interpretation. Avoid wall-clock seeds, unordered iteration, hidden random choices, and locale-sensitive sorting. Include a late-arrival replay and a missing-record replay so optional content cannot alter the deterministic core unexpectedly.

#### Extended field 14 — UI and accessibility

The UI exposes a compact action label, expanded explanation, cost, consequence preview, focus order, keyboard and controller back behavior, readable long text, contrast, scaling, non-color cues, and confirmation for irreversible choices. Provide an audio or text alternative. If a record is missing, show a truthful unavailable state and preserve navigation. Archive and map panels consume projections; they do not own decisions.

#### Extended field 15 — Performance and lifecycle

Set budgets for catalog parse, query, event dispatch, archive projection, panel refresh, long text, and return visits. Load high-volume rows lazily, page them without changing order, dispose listeners on close, and avoid repeated full-catalog scans. Add one degradation path for a missing asset or provider. Note the smallest focused host smoke needed if the owner route is eventually implemented.

#### Extended field 16 — Acceptance and handoff

Acceptance requires premise evidence, owner and consumer proof, one reachable player command, save round trip, migration fixture, paired replay, accessibility review, performance notes, and a rollback boundary. The handoff names untouched shared paths and labels this as design scaffolding. The final image is practical: a repaired latch, an amended map, a divided bowl, a chalk mark, a quiet signal, or a door left open by consent.
